title: Insertion Sort vs Merge Sort
q: Which sort finishes first: insertion sort or merge sort?
r1res: 6 items: insertion 23 steps, merge 26. Insertion leads until the 10-item list
r2: All nine lists, up to 256 items
rule: Insertion sort (O(n²)) wins on tiny lists; merge sort (O(n log n)) wins as lists grow. Python's own sort uses both.
iq: Why would a real sort use insertion sort at all?
ia: On a handful of items it does less work than merge sort, so libraries sort short runs with it and merge the runs (CPython's list sort does this).
setup: Counted steps, not timed: you should get exactly these numbers on any machine. One step is one comparison or one array write. For each size, a typical shuffle (closest to the average of 2,000), seed 19.

title: Linear Scan vs Binary Search
q: Searching 128 items 64 times: linear scan or binary search?
r1res: Binary search spends them sorting and finds nothing; the scan is already finding items
r2res: Binary 2,343 steps (sort included); scan 4,116. When binary finished, scan had found 34
rule: Search once: just scan. Search a lot: sort first, then binary search. That is why databases keep sorted indexes.
iq: When is binary search not worth it?
ia: When you search only once or twice: sorting costs more than the scans you save. It pays off over many searches.
setup: Counted steps, not timed: you should get exactly these numbers on any machine. One step is one comparison or one array write. A typical draw of list and targets (closest to the average of 3,000), seed 20.

title: DFS vs BFS
q: Escaping a maze: depth-first or breadth-first search?
r1res: DFS after 75 cells checked, BFS after 136
r2res: BFS's route is 35 cells (the shortest); DFS's is 57
rule: Any way out: DFS. The shortest way: BFS. Over 3,000 mazes, DFS got out first in 94% and took the longer route in 94%.
iq: Why does BFS always find the shortest path in an unweighted grid?
ia: It checks every cell 1 step away, then 2, then 3, so the first time it reaches the exit is by the fewest steps.
setup: Counted steps, not timed: you should get exactly these numbers on any machine. One step is one cell taken off the stack or queue. 13 x 13 maze with a few loops, a typical one of 3,000, seed 25.

title: Dijkstra vs A*
q: On real city roads, which finds the shortest route with less work: Dijkstra or A*?
r1: Junctions checked, MG Road metro to Indiranagar metro (Bengaluru)
rule: A* adds one guess, the straight-line distance to the goal. It still finds the shortest route, with far less searching.
iq: Why is A* still guaranteed the shortest route?
ia: Its guess, the straight-line distance, is never longer than the real road distance, so it never skips a shorter path.
setup: Counted steps, not timed: you should get exactly these numbers on any machine. One step is one junction taken off the queue. Roads: OpenStreetMap data read on 6 Nov 2026, included as osm.json (© OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL). Fresh downloads can differ slightly.

title: O(1) vs O(2ⁿ)
q: Same 60 numbers, five algorithms: how many steps does each take?
r1: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n²) on 60 numbers
r2: O(2ⁿ): try every subset of the 60
r2res: 2⁶⁰ subsets: about 36.5 years at a billion a second
rule: The O tells you how the work grows: one more number doubles O(2ⁿ), adds about 120 steps to O(n²), and changes nothing for O(1).
iq: Two numbers that add up to a target: how do you beat O(n²)?
ia: Remember the numbers you have seen in a dict and check for target minus x: one pass, O(n).
setup: Counted steps, not timed: you should get exactly these numbers on any machine. The O(2ⁿ) lane is run for real on 10, 16 and 20 numbers to show it is exactly 2ⁿ; 60 is calculated.

title: CPU vs GPU
q: Which is faster, the CPU or the GPU?
r1res: GPU 14 ms, CPU 162 ms: GPU 11x faster
r2: 10,000 steps, each needing the step before (x = x * 0.999 + 1)
r2res: CPU 36 ms, GPU 156 ms: CPU 4x faster
rule: Work that splits into independent pieces goes to the GPU; work that runs step by step stays on the CPU.
iq: Why do AI models run on GPUs?
ia: They are mostly huge matrix multiplies, where every output cell can be computed at the same time.
run: pip install torch   # a CUDA build, with an NVIDIA GPU
setup: Intel Core i9-14900HX laptop with an NVIDIA RTX 4070 Laptop GPU, PyTorch 2.8, median of 3 runs.

title: Sort All vs Heap of 10
q: Top 10 out of 1,000,000 scores: sort everything or keep a heap of 10?
r2res: Heap 21 ms, sort 151 ms (one laptop; times vary)
rule: For the top K of anything, keep a heap of size K: one comparison per item for most items. In Python: heapq.nlargest(10, scores).
iq: Find the K largest numbers in a huge list.
ia: Keep a min-heap of K; replace its smallest whenever a bigger number arrives. O(n log K) instead of O(n log n) for a full sort.
setup: The comparison counts are counted, not timed, and match on any machine (seed 34). The milliseconds are from one Intel Core i9-14900HX laptop, Python 3.10, median of 3, and will differ on yours.

title: Python vs C
q: Which is faster, Python or C?
r1: Add up the squares of 100,000,000 numbers in a plain loop
r1res: C 63 ms, Python 3,882 ms: C 62x faster
r2: Same job, Python makes one NumPy call: np.dot(a, a)
rule: A plain Python loop is slow; one library call that runs the loop in compiled code is fast.
iq: Why is Python slow, and why is it still used for AI?
ia: The interpreter runs a loop one step at a time; the heavy loops in AI run in compiled code underneath (NumPy, PyTorch).
setup: Intel Core i9-14900HX laptop, Python 3.10, NumPy 1.26, gcc 13.3 with -O2, median of 7 runs.

title: RAM vs SSD
q: Which is faster, RAM or an SSD?
r1: Look up 100,000 records of 4 KB at random places in the same 1 GB
r1res: RAM 46 ms, SSD 11,249 ms: RAM 245x faster
r2: The program holding the data is killed (kill -9)
r2res: RAM: 0 bytes left. SSD file: all 1,073,741,824 bytes back, same checksum
rule: RAM is fast but forgets; disk is slow but remembers. Real systems use both.
iq: Why do databases write a log to disk before changing data?
ia: So that after a crash they can rebuild every change from the log; memory is wiped when the process dies.
run: ./ramssd mkfile data.bin          # writes a 1 GB test file here
./ramssd rnd-ssd data.bin 100000   # reads straight from the drive (O_DIRECT, Linux)
setup: Intel Core i9-14900HX laptop, NVMe SSD read from Linux inside WSL2 (which adds some delay to every disk request), gcc -O2, median of 5 runs. Round 1 reads with the system's in-memory copy switched off; read the normal way after one full read, the same lookups took about 58 ms.

title: Threads vs Processes
q: In Python, which is faster: threads or processes?
r1: 8 jobs of pure maths, all started at once
r1res: 8 processes 132 ms, 8 threads 702 ms: processes 5.3x faster
r2: 1,000 tiny jobs, a new worker started for each
r2res: Threads 65 ms, processes 1,124 ms: threads 17x faster
rule: Heavy calculation goes to processes; many small or waiting jobs go to threads.
ia: In standard Python only one thread runs Python code at a time. Threads still help while waiting on files or the network, and they are cheap to start.
setup: Intel Core i9-14900HX laptop (20 cores), Python 3.10 on Linux, standard build with the GIL, median of 5 runs.

title: Index vs No Index
q: In SQL, is a table faster with an index or without?
r1: Find one user by email among 5,000,000
r1res: With index 0.0031 ms, without 121 ms: about 39,000x faster
r2res: Without index 507 ms, with index 920 ms: 1.8x faster; the index also doubled the file (191 MB to 381 MB)
rule: Lots of reads: add the index. Lots of writes: keep indexes few.
ia: Each index makes every insert and update slower and takes disk space.
run: python3 race.py .     # creates and deletes two test databases in the given folder (about 600 MB at peak)
setup: Intel Core i9-14900HX laptop, SQLite 3.52 from Python, median of 3 runs, lookup is the best of 5.

title: Array vs Linked List
q: Which is faster, an array or a linked list?
r1res: Array 5.3 ms, shuffled linked list 1,060 ms
r2: Insert 2,000 values at the front of 200,000
rule: Arrays win at reading in order (the CPU fetches neighbours together); linked lists win at inserting at the front.
iq: Why is a linked list slow to walk even though each step is O(1)?
ia: Its nodes are scattered in memory, so almost every step is a cache miss; an array's values sit next to each other.
setup: Intel Core i9-14900HX laptop, gcc -O2, median of 5 runs (14 Nov 2026).
